# What Do You Want to Become in Future?

[Silas Bambil · November 2026]{.meta}

Shortly after my accident in 2021, I came across an observation that has stayed with me ever since: “Be conscious of the role of chance in your life and understand that your success isn’t completely deserved, neither is the failure of others.” Perhaps the circumstances under which I encountered those words made them particularly meaningful. Before my accident, I had plans for the next few years of my life and every intention of pursuing them. For all the thought I had given to my future, I had never considered the possibility of having to learn how to walk again. The years that followed would give those words even greater meaning.

One of the most uncomfortable things I have come to accept about life is that you can do all the right things and still fail. Equally, you can succeed without having done much to deserve that success. As someone who has devoted years to education and personal development, I find this reality particularly frustrating. I would like to believe that if I work sufficiently hard, make sensible decisions, and prepare adequately, things will eventually unfold in my favour. Unfortunately, life has never entered into such an agreement with me. There are circumstances against which even the most careful preparation offers little protection.

Perhaps this explains why I consider “What do you want to become in future?” to be among the dumbest questions we routinely ask children, particularly when we expect them to provide a definitive answer. What exactly has a child experienced at that point to make such an important decision? How many professions have they encountered? How much do they understand about the work these professions entail? A child may want to become a doctor simply because doctors are among the few professionals they know. Meanwhile, somewhere in the world is a profession they might thoroughly enjoy but will not discover for another fifteen years.

Much of what interests us is influenced by our socialisation. Our teachers, families, friends, and the opportunities available to us all contribute to what we find interesting and what we consider possible. A teacher can make a previously uninteresting subject fascinating, and an unexpected opportunity can reveal an ability we never knew we possessed. Yet we ask children to identify what they want to become before many of these experiences have occurred. I find nothing wrong with encouraging children to have ambitions. What amuses me is the seriousness with which we sometimes regard their answers.

I wanted to become an engineer when I was younger. That ambition seemed perfectly reasonable to me until my science teacher in Junior High School contributed to my losing interest in science. I sometimes wonder whether I would have continued pursuing engineering had I encountered a teacher who made the subject enjoyable. There is no reliable way of knowing. Nevertheless, I find it fascinating that something I had once been sufficiently enthusiastic about to imagine pursuing professionally could lose its appeal through my experience with a teacher. So much for knowing what I wanted to become.

Then I wanted to become a politician. I genuinely loved politics and could imagine pursuing a life in it. Considering some of the things I have subsequently written about political culture, I find that particular ambition rather amusing. At the time, however, politics interested me enormously. I had no reason to believe that my enthusiasm would eventually diminish or that I would discover other things that I found considerably more interesting. Had someone asked me about my future during that period, I would probably have answered with as much conviction as when I wanted to become an engineer.

My Elective Mathematics teacher subsequently made me fall in love with mathematics. The contrast between my experiences with these two teachers has always interested me. One contributed to my losing enthusiasm for a subject, while the other helped me discover something that would influence much of my education. Neither the science nor the mathematics had changed. What had changed was my experience of learning them. The child who wanted to become an engineer had not yet encountered the teacher who would make him love mathematics. How was I supposed to know what I would enjoy before someone had introduced me to it?

My interest in mathematics eventually developed into an interest in finance and risk management. I found these disciplines fascinating and could imagine spending much of my professional life pursuing them. I invested years in acquiring academic qualifications, developing my abilities, and pursuing professional credentials. For a while, it appeared that I had finally arrived at a reasonably convincing answer to the question of what I wanted to become. Interestingly, some of the things I was now so enthusiastic about were things I barely knew existed as a child. And even this was not the end of my changing interests.

After moving to America in 2023, I continued to encounter circumstances that reminded me of that observation about chance. I eventually found myself teaching in a high school because that was the opportunity available to me. Teaching had not occupied a particularly prominent place in my professional plans, yet I developed a genuine interest in it. Had another opportunity been available to me at the time, I might have taken it and never discovered how much I enjoyed teaching. In this instance, what I wanted to do professionally was influenced by what I happened to have the opportunity to do.

Unfortunately, I had to leave teaching because of circumstances connected to my F-1 student status. I found this particularly frustrating. I had discovered something I genuinely enjoyed doing, only to find myself unable to continue doing it for reasons that had little to do with my interest in the work or my ability to perform it. Until then, much of my uncertainty had concerned what I wanted to do. Now, I was confronted with a different problem altogether. I knew that I enjoyed teaching, but knowing that did very little to change the circumstances that required me to leave.

Then came my growing interest in research. I discovered that I genuinely enjoyed investigating problems, developing ideas, and trying to understand things that were not immediately apparent. Research now occupies a considerable amount of my attention. But given my history, I would be rather presumptuous to announce that I have finally discovered what I want to spend the rest of my life doing. The aspiring engineer, the aspiring politician, and the person who became interested in teaching would probably all have made similarly confident declarations at different points in my life. I have learnt to be somewhat suspicious of my own certainty.

There is also something rather amusing about having devoted so much of my education to studying uncertainty, probability, and risk management while possessing remarkably little certainty about my own future. I have spent years learning how to make decisions when outcomes are uncertain, yet some of the most important questions concerning my own life remain unanswered. Apparently, acquiring an education in risk management does not exempt one from having a rather risky and unpredictable existence. If nothing else, my personal circumstances have given me a rather intimate appreciation of the subject matter.

I have academic qualifications and professional credentials, yet I continue to struggle to secure employment. My F-1 student status is among the circumstances that have complicated my search for opportunities. What frustrates me is knowing that I could spend another year studying, pass another professional examination, or become considerably better at what I do and still encounter some of the same obstacles. For someone accustomed to addressing his shortcomings through education and preparation, this is particularly difficult to accept. There is a difference between being qualified to perform a job and being in circumstances that allow you to obtain it.

These experiences have changed how I regard the success and failure of other people. I am less inclined to assume that someone who has achieved considerable professional success must have worked harder than someone who is still struggling. Some people have encountered opportunities that allowed their abilities to flourish, while others have spent years trying to obtain comparable opportunities. When I think about my accident, I am reminded that there were people whose plans remained uninterrupted without their having done anything particularly clever to avoid what happened to me. How much of what we congratulate ourselves for might have been different had our circumstances been slightly less favourable?

And here I am, pushing thirty. I have no job, no wife, and no children. My professional future remains uncertain, and after all the different things I have wanted to become, I am not entirely sure what I want to become anymore. I had imagined having a much clearer understanding of my life by this age. I would have liked to know where my career was going, to have some financial stability, and to be in a position to make plans about starting a family. These are things that genuinely matter to me, and I would be lying if I said their absence did not sometimes bother me.

It is not as though I have run out of things I want to do. I still enjoy mathematics, finance, teaching, and research. I would love to get married, have children, and establish a comfortable life for myself and my family. What I cannot tell you is how these things will eventually come together. I do not know which opportunities will become available to me or what new interests I might discover. Given how much my interests have changed over the years, I suspect there are still things I would thoroughly enjoy doing that I have simply not encountered yet.

Perhaps I would be more interested in asking a child what they enjoy doing, what they are curious about, or what they would like to learn. I would certainly find those answers more meaningful than a declaration about the profession they intend to pursue twenty years later. When I was a child, I could confidently tell you that I wanted to become an engineer. I knew nothing about the accident that would interrupt my plans, the professions I would eventually discover, or the circumstances that would complicate my employment prospects. Yet, rather amusingly, the little boy who knew almost nothing about life could answer a question that I, with all this education and experience, can no longer answer.

What do I want to become in future? I honestly do not know.

*The original thought that inspired this reflection occurred to me on 19 June 2021 at 18:04 EST, shortly after my accident.*
